# 2025 Somerset–London Tornado

## Meteorological Profile and Track

The 2025 Somerset–London tornado was a powerful and destructive mesoscale convective system that left a clear and devastating mark on southeastern Kentucky . The event's meteorological characteristics are defined by its intensity, duration, and extensive path length, making it a significant subject for post-storm analysis and historical record. A critical point of clarification arises from conflicting reports regarding the exact date of the tornado's occurrence. One set of sources indicates the tornado formed on May 16, 2025, at 10:26 p.m. Eastern Daylight Time (EDT) and dissipated around 11:56 p.m. EDT on the same day . This timeline is supported by granular data detailing its duration of one hour and thirty minutes and its officially confirmed classification , . Another source places the event on December 12-13, 2025, describing an initial touchdown in Somerset around 11 p.m. on Friday, followed by a second wave impacting London shortly after midnight on Saturday, December 13 . Given the high level of technical detail and the mention of a formal post-event confirmation process in the May account, this timeline appears more substantiated; however, the discrepancy highlights the challenges in establishing a precise chronology immediately following a catastrophic event. For the purpose of this report, the detailed May 16 timeline will be used as the primary basis for the meteorological profile.

The official assessment by the National Weather Service Jackson, Kentucky, classified the tornado as an EF4 on the Enhanced Fujita scale, signifying a violent storm with catastrophic potential . This rating reflects an estimated peak wind speed of 170 miles per hour (270 kilometers per hour) . The EF4 classification indicates that the tornado was capable of causing complete destruction of well-built homes and entire communities, with large missiles being thrown considerable distances and vehicles being lifted and carried. It is important to note that this rating was not a preliminary estimate but a conclusion reached after a comprehensive damage survey conducted by meteorologists . Initially, the tornado was rated as EF3, but several days after the event, the survey findings led to an upgrade to the higher EF4 category, underscoring the rigorous process required to accurately assess tornado intensity based on observed damage patterns , . The storm's immense power is further evidenced by its ability to traverse vast distances and diverse terrains, including both urbanized areas and dense forestland .

The tornado's path was exceptionally long, stretching approximately 60.02 miles (96.59 kilometers) from its point of origin to its dissipation . An alternative source provides a slightly different but comparable figure, estimating the track length at around 60 miles . This extended path allowed the tornado to maintain its structure and intensity for a remarkable duration of one hour and thirty minutes . Such longevity is characteristic of a highly organized and stable supercell thunderstorm, capable of producing multiple vortices and maintaining a continuous supply of energy over a broad geographical area. The tornado's trajectory began in Somerset, located in Pulaski County, and moved southeastward toward the city of London in Laurel County, a distance of roughly 75 miles south of Lexington, Kentucky's capital city , . This direct path through two distinct counties defines the core scope of the tornado's impact zone. The storm's ability to travel deep into the Daniel Boone National Forest, a significant portion of its journey, demonstrates its capacity to inflict widespread ecological damage, a factor later assessed using specialized satellite imagery techniques that tracked persistent disturbances in forest canopy structure . The combination of its EF4 intensity, nearly two-hour duration, and a 60-mile-long path classifies the 2025 Somerset–London tornado as a major, long-track, high-intensity event, placing it among the most severe tornadoes documented in the region's recent history.

## Geographic Impact and Damage Assessment

The geographic footprint of the 2025 Somerset–London tornado was extensive, tracing a direct line of destruction from Somerset through London and into surrounding rural areas . The storm's path began in the city of Somerset, situated in Pulaski County, where initial reports indicated a possible tornado touched down around 11 p.m. on the night of May 15th (the evening prior to its formation on May 16th according to the primary timeline) . From Somerset, the tornado traveled southeast, crossing into Laurel County and making a direct hit on the city of London, which lies approximately 75 miles south of Lexington , . This progression along a relatively straight axis ensured that both communities experienced the full force of the EF4-rated winds. The tornado's reach extended beyond the primary urban centers, impacting rural areas in both Pulaski and Laurel Counties, and even affecting parts of Russell County, as noted in the distribution of casualties , . The sheer length of its track, spanning nearly 60 miles, meant that the damage was not confined to a single location but unfolded sequentially along its path, creating a swath of devastation across three separate counties , .

The structural damage caused by the tornado was catastrophic and widespread. The official count revealed that a total of 1,500 homes were either damaged or completely destroyed across the affected regions . This massive number points to a mass casualty incident, a term formally declared by Laurel County authorities in response to the overwhelming scale of the disaster . The intensity of the EF4 winds was sufficient to level entire neighborhoods, particularly in London, where drone footage captured flattened homes and overturned vehicles, providing a stark visual testament to the storm's power . The destruction was not limited to residential properties; mobile homes were also destroyed, highlighting the vulnerability of certain housing types to such extreme events . One of the most compelling pieces of evidence for the tornado's ferocity came from the Sunshine Hills Baptist Church in London, whose complete destruction was confirmed during a subsequent damage survey and cited as a key factor in upgrading the tornado's rating to EF4 .

In addition to residential and religious structures, the tornado inflicted significant damage on critical infrastructure. The London-Corbin Airport was severely impacted, with a medical helicopter being destroyed and at least one airplane being pulled into the funnel cloud, illustrating the immense lifting force of the vortex . The Somerset Fire Department issued urgent warnings via social media about downed power lines and poles, indicating that the electrical grid suffered extensive disruption, a common consequence of such storms that can hinder emergency response and prolong recovery efforts . Beyond man-made structures, the tornado's passage through the Daniel Boone National Forest demonstrated its ability to cause profound ecological damage . Satellite-based assessments relied on identifying persistent disturbances in the forest canopy, such as delayed green-up or multi-year crown damage, to map the extent of the destruction in these remote areas . The evergreen conifer species like pine and hemlock served as year-round indicators of structural damage, allowing for a detailed analysis of the tornado's impact on the natural landscape . The combination of destroyed homes, damaged infrastructure, and ecological harm paints a picture of an event with far-reaching consequences that affected every aspect of life in its path.

## Human Toll and Casualty Report

The human cost of the 2025 Somerset–London tornado was tragically high, with a final confirmed death toll of twenty individuals . The casualty count was not static in the immediate aftermath of the disaster; it evolved as emergency responders searched through the wreckage and medical teams treated the wounded. Initially, the reported death toll was at least nineteen people, with seventeen fatalities confirmed in Laurel County alone, specifically within the city of London , . Other early reports placed the total at seventeen deaths, also noting one fatality in rural Pulaski County and one in Russell County, with another casualty remaining unconfirmed , . The uncertainty surrounding the initial figures is typical of major disaster events, where access to all affected areas is difficult and some victims may succumb to their injuries days or even weeks later. The final, confirmed death toll of twenty was reached after several days, with the twentieth fatality being officially confirmed on June 5, 2025, solidifying the event's place as a major loss-of-life incident . The possibility that the death toll could rise further was acknowledged by officials in the immediate wake of the storm, as critically injured victims were still in intensive care .

The distribution of these tragic losses provides a sobering breakdown of the tornado's localized impact across the three counties it traversed. The majority of the fatalities occurred in Laurel County, which bore the brunt of the storm's impact as it passed directly through London , . Specifically, sixteen of the nineteen initially reported deaths were in London, highlighting the intense devastation experienced in the city center , . The remaining three confirmed fatalities were spread out geographically: one in rural Pulaski County, one in Russell County, and one casualty that was initially unconfirmed , . This geographic dispersion underscores that while the epicenter of destruction was in London, the tornado's powerful winds and associated hazards extended far beyond the city limits, claiming lives in surrounding rural communities as well. The final confirmation of the twentieth victim brought closure to families and provided a definitive measure of the tragedy's scale, though the emotional and psychological toll on survivors and first responders would continue for years to come.

Beyond the fatalities, the tornado resulted in at least one hundred and eight injuries, adding to the immense strain on the region's healthcare system . These injuries ranged from minor cuts and bruises sustained from flying debris to severe trauma requiring hospitalization. The sheer volume of injured individuals overwhelmed local medical facilities, necessitating coordination with regional hospitals and emergency medical services to provide adequate care. The high number of casualties and injuries, combined with the widespread destruction of 1,500 homes, collectively justified the declaration of a mass casualty incident by Laurel County authorities . This designation mobilizes additional resources and establishes protocols for managing a disaster that exceeds the normal capacity of local emergency services. The human toll—twenty dead and over a hundred injured—serves as a grim reminder of the destructive power of violent tornadoes and the profound and lasting impact such events have on communities, families, and individuals.

## Response, Recovery, and Relief Operations

The response to the 2025 Somerset–London tornado was a complex, multi-layered effort involving local, state, and federal agencies, alongside a wide array of non-governmental organizations (NGOs) and charitable groups. In the immediate aftermath of the storm, local emergency services were the first to respond. The Somerset Fire Department played a crucial role by utilizing social media platforms to issue timely warnings to the public, advising residents of the dangers posed by downed power lines and poles . This real-time communication was vital for preventing secondary accidents and ensuring public safety in the hazardous environment created by the tornado. On the ground, Mayor Randall Weddle of London provided firsthand accounts of the scene, describing the devastation as "overwhelming" and offering a personal perspective on the scale of the disaster that gripped the community . These local actions, while critical, were quickly augmented by a broader coordinated effort aimed at search and rescue, securing affected areas, and beginning the initial stages of sheltering displaced residents.

At the state level, the involvement of Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear was significant. He personally toured the tornado-damaged areas in Laurel County by both car and helicopter on the day following the storm, demonstrating leadership and solidarity with the affected communities . During his visit, he acknowledged the severity of the situation, stating that the event represented the thirteenth major weather disaster to strike the state during his tenure . His tour was not merely symbolic; it was part of a strategic effort to coordinate with federal emergency management leaders and DHS Secretary Kristi Noem to secure funding and resources for both short-term relief and long-term recovery . This state-level engagement was essential for organizing a systematic response and communicating the needs of the affected counties to the highest levels of government.

Federal intervention was swift and decisive. On May 23, 2025, President Joe Biden officially declared a Presidential Disaster Declaration for the six counties most affected by the tornado, designated as Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Major Disaster Declaration DR-4875-KY . This declaration unlocked a vast array of federal assistance programs, including Individual Assistance for displaced homeowners and renters, Public Assistance for repairing public infrastructure like roads and bridges, and Hazard Mitigation grants to help communities rebuild stronger and more resiliently. The declaration covered a wider area than just the tornado's direct path, encompassing Pulaski, Laurel, and Russell Counties, as well as three others, recognizing the widespread nature of the damage and economic disruption . The recovery effort was then led by FEMA in partnership with numerous other entities, including The Salvation Army, Operation Barbecue Relief, Samaritan's Purse, and the Team Kentucky Storm Relief Fund . This diverse coalition of organizations provided a spectrum of support, from immediate food and shelter to long-term rebuilding and spiritual counseling, reflecting the multifaceted nature of recovery from a catastrophic event. The extensive involvement of this ecosystem of governmental and non-governmental actors demonstrates the event's significant impact and the collective response required to aid a community in its time of need.

## Economic Consequences and Disaster Declaration

The economic fallout from the 2025 Somerset–London tornado was substantial, measured in the hundreds of millions of dollars and extending far beyond the immediate destruction of property. The most concrete financial figure available pertains specifically to Laurel County, where the direct damage was estimated at $350 million in 2025 U.S. dollars . This staggering sum represents the cost of repairing and rebuilding the 1,500 homes that were damaged or destroyed, as well as the restoration of public infrastructure, businesses, and other structures within the county . While this figure provides a clear snapshot of the economic burden on Laurel County, it is important to note that the total statewide damage was undoubtedly much higher. The tornado's path crossed into Pulaski and Russell Counties, and the subsequent Presidential Disaster Declaration (DR-4875-KY) encompassed six counties in total, indicating that the full economic impact rippled across a broad region of eastern Kentucky . The true statewide economic toll, including lost business revenue, job displacement, and the costs of long-term recovery, remains a larger figure yet to be fully calculated.

The declaration of a major disaster by the federal government was a pivotal moment in the economic recovery process. The Presidential Disaster Declaration DR-4875-KY, issued on May 23, 2025, was the mechanism through which federal funds were channeled to assist the affected communities . This declaration authorized FEMA to provide various forms of financial assistance. Under the Individual Assistance program, eligible residents could receive grants to cover temporary housing, home repairs, and other serious disaster-related expenses not covered by insurance. The Public Assistance program provided matching funds to state, tribal, and local governments, as well as certain private nonprofit organizations, to reimburse them for repairing or replacing disaster-damaged public infrastructure, such as roads, water systems, and schools . Furthermore, the declaration enabled the Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP), which provides funding to implement measures that will reduce the risk of future disaster damage to public and private structures. This program is crucial for helping communities rebuild in a way that enhances resilience against future storms, potentially mitigating the economic impact of similar events in the long run. The scale of the disaster declaration itself, covering six counties, underscores that the economic devastation was not isolated to a single municipality but was a regional crisis requiring a coordinated and comprehensive federal response.

The economic consequences of the tornado extend beyond the immediate repair costs. The destruction of 1,500 homes represents a significant blow to the housing market and the overall economy of the affected counties . Many residents were left homeless, leading to a surge in demand for rental properties and temporary housing solutions, which can drive up prices in the short term. Businesses that were destroyed or damaged faced prolonged closures, resulting in lost wages for employees and reduced tax revenues for local governments. The disruption to the workforce and supply chains can have a cascading effect on the regional economy. The declaration of a mass casualty incident and the significant human toll of 20 fatalities and 108 injuries also impose a heavy societal and economic cost related to healthcare and long-term care for survivors . Therefore, the $350 million figure for Laurel County is merely the tip of the iceberg when considering the full economic impact, which includes long-term unemployment, reduced consumer spending, and the investment required to restore the region's economic vitality to its pre-disaster state.

A violent, tornado-spawning storm system tore across the central US, leaving at least 25 people dead in Missouri and southeastern Kentucky as it cut a path of destruction through several states.

The storm made its way towards Kansas and Oklahoma late Sunday, where significant damage was reported in Grinnell, a town some 250 miles west of Wichita. Photos show severely damaged homes, blocked roads and overturned vehicles. One image shows a local church with its roof blown off.

Parts of the I-70 and Kansas Highway northwest of the state have been closed due to downed power lines near Grinnell, according to roadway tracker [KanDrive](https://www.kandrive.gov/event/CARS5-8552/@-100.66092,38.69799,7?show=roadReports,constructionReports,trafficSpeeds,oversizeLoads,stationsAlert,weatherRadar).

In the small town of Plevna, roughly 60 miles from Wichita, Reno County Sheriff Darrian Campbell said a passing tornado Sunday night caused significant damage to homes.

“We did have a tornado touch down and travel approximately 12 miles and went through a small town of Plevna,” Campbell said in an email to CNN.

There are no reports of injuries in Kansas, where a life-threatening tornado alert was issued for the cities of [Sylvia, Plevna, and Abbyville](https://x.com/nwstornado/status/1924326970684248161?s=46&t=fixpKyW5AlkbVtQIbFqgMw) until roughly midnight CST. CNN has reached out to state authorities for more details.

Over the weekend, 18 deaths were reported in Kentucky, just hours after authorities announced seven [fatalities](https://www.cnn.com/2025/05/16/weather/tornadoes-severe-weather-wind-climate) in the St. Louis, Missouri area.

Two additional deaths were reported in northern Virginia. Both fatalities were caused by trees falling onto vehicles, one in Fairfax County and another on the George Washington Memorial Parkway, Fairfax County police and the United States Park Police said.

The storms damaged homes and downed power lines across the Midwest and Great Lakes, brought by the same system that produced [destructive storms and tornadoes Thursday](https://www.cnn.com/2025/05/15/weather/tornado-severe-storms-midwest-east-climate).

Over 100,000 homes and businesses across five states were without power as of Sunday night, with Missouri, Michigan and Arkansas among the hardest hit, according to [Poweroutage.us](https://poweroutage.us/).

The same storm system hit Colorado Sunday afternoon, producing at least two tornadoes. Homes and buildings in Arapahoe, Adams and Elbert County were damaged or lost, according the counties’ sheriff’s offices. No injuries were reported.

It’s part of a multiday spate of widespread severe weather stretching into early next week. As the system that generated deadly tornadoes in Missouri and Kentucky loses strength, another round of severe storms is expected near the border with Mexico, thrusting more than 20 million Americans across the Southwest in the risk zone.

![Image 1: Grier Allen carries Lynn White's pet turtle in a plastic bin from what is left of White's home in London, Kentucky, on Saturday.](https://media.cnn.com/api/v1/images/stellar/prod/ap25137748530455.jpg?c=original&q=w_860,c_fill)

The National Weather Service reported a radar-confirmed, “large, extremely dangerous” tornado sweeping east across lower Kentucky shortly after midnight.

Video and photos from southeastern Kentucky show a trail of destruction that began in Pulaski County before moving east into neighboring Laurel County, leaving at least 18 dead and 10 in critical condition across the state. Videos [showed](https://www.facebook.com/laurelcountyfiscalcourt/videos/1030447172529945/?rdid=ocHGj7CY1F9l0k4Y) widespread damage to buildings, cars, trees and infrastructure in the wake of the possible tornado.

“I’ve now been governor for at least 14 federally declared disasters, 13 of them weather. And this is one of the worst,” Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear said at a news conference Saturday evening. “It’s one of the worst in terms of the loss of human life. It’s one of the worst in terms of damage.”

Beshear has declared a state of emergency in the state and requested a federal disaster declaration.

Mahala Watts told CNN [affiliate WLKY](https://www.wlky.com/article/kentucky-tornado-deaths-laurel-county-survivors-search/64799829) her family was watching the news after 11 p.m. Friday when their phones started blaring with tornado warnings. She grabbed the dog, and her family took cover in the bathroom in the center of their home in Laurel County.

The storm suddenly roared over her house – as the family was “breathing in all the debris.” They got on their hands and knees, Watts told the station. A bathroom mirror fell on Watts before the roar went silent.

“We were just kind of praying, you know, scared it was going to come back,” she said. “We had no idea the roof was gone. The fridge was blocking the bathroom door.”

Watts told WLKY her family climbed over the refrigerator and stood outside in the dark, fearing another hit. Cars were overturned and debris was strewn about. They used a relative’s car to get to a hospital where they sought refuge before making it to a hotel after the storm passed.

![Image 2: Damage from a Friday night storm is seen at the London-Corbin Airport in London, Kentucky, on Saturday.](https://media.cnn.com/api/v1/images/stellar/prod/still-21631906-302277-172-still.jpg?c=original&q=w_860,c_fill)

Drone video over London, Kentucky, at daylight Saturday showed a vast wasteland of damaged and overturned vehicles and flattened homes as first responders searched heaps of rubble for possible survivors. London is about 75 miles south of Lexington.

At the London-Corbin Airport, several planes were damaged and a medical helicopter was destroyed, [CNN affiliate WLKY](https://www.wlky.com/article/aerials-tornado-airport-london-corbin-kentucky-damage/64801129) reported, adding officials said at least one airplane was pulled into a funnel cloud. Hangars and other buildings were leveled.

In another video from Laurel County, first responders are seen descending on the Sunshine Hills area, a barren landscape of twisted cars, downed trees and piles of debris.

Seventeen deaths were reported in Laurel County, including in London, Mayor Randall Weddle told [CNN affiliate WKYT.](https://www.wkyt.com/2025/05/17/multiple-dead-after-possible-tornado-london-mayor-says/) Among those who died was Maj. Leslie Roger Leatherman of the [Laurel County Fire Department](https://www.facebook.com/laurelcountyfd/posts/pfbid0oNeLhXW6VNtkujtAvw4mHLrQg787Shm4fyRsKNG8Bp5WTe74siv6FQ5bVP8XseZNl), who had been responding to the storm, the governor said Saturday.

“I have never personally witnessed what I’ve witnessed here tonight. There’s a lot of devastation,” Weddle told WKYT.

Police in Corbin, south of London, were responding to mutual aid calls for tornado victims and [described](https://www.facebook.com/watch/?v=1210058197581617&rdid=1vmj8SjYryJRnCj0) the devastation as overwhelming.

“Stop and pray for Laurel County residents and victims of the tornado that touched down there,” the department wrote.

Pulaski County Judge Executive Marshall Todd declared a state of emergency, and crews are working on cleanup efforts, county spokesperson John Alexander told CNN. One person was reported dead in the county.

Heavy damage can be seen in Somerset, a city in Pulaski County to the west of London, where emergency officials urged residents to stay indoors.

“The southern side of the city has been hit by a possible tornado!” the Somerset Fire Department [posted on social media](https://www.facebook.com/SomersetfiredeptKY/posts/pfbid02BbDNyZypV4ZBCLGmzZ59LBENHtv6z3PoALSrfuWSZgSuCKexhcycVK76Fb4GHSzpl) around 11 p.m. Friday. “Please avoid the area, poles and power lines are down!”

![Image 3: A large tree blocks a road after a severe storm moved through St. Louis on Friday.](https://media.cnn.com/api/v1/images/stellar/prod/ap25136844377573.jpg?c=original&q=w_860,c_fill)

A storm that produced a devastating tornado in the St. Louis area Friday afternoon has left five people dead and many others injured, according to local authorities. The EF3 tornado traveled at least 8 miles, according to an [initial survey](https://x.com/NWSStLouis/status/1923892902293344467) conducted by the National Weather Service.

“We’re just a city that’s really grieving,” the city’s new mayor, Cara Spencer, told reporters Saturday. About 5,000 buildings have been impacted by the severe weather but she noted, “This community is coming together in a truly, truly amazing way.”

Spencer called the event “one of the worst storms” in the city’s history. A curfew will remain in place overnight and thousands of homes and businesses still have no power. Nearly 40 people were injured, the mayor said. A state of emergency was declared in the city, and officials are seeking a federal major disaster declaration.

More than 130 miles to the south of St. Louis, in Scott County, [two others were killed](https://www.facebook.com/Sheriff63736/posts/122246320412070531?ref=embed_post) during Friday’s storms, Sheriff Derick Wheetley announced on social media. Several others were taken to medical facilities, “with injuries ranging from minor to severe,” the sheriff added.

“The tornado moved from the eastern part of the county, leaving behind a trail of destruction, with multiple homes completely lost and areas left unrecognizable,” the sheriff said.

The devastation occurred after a tornado warning was issued at 2:34 p.m. Friday and a “likely tornado” touched down seven to eight minutes later, said Ben Herzog, a science and operations officer with the National Weather Service.

One St. Louis resident**,** Cindy Spellman, told CNN her niece was in her apartment when the storm hit.

![Image 4: Damage from the Friday storm is seen in St. Louis.](https://media.cnn.com/api/v1/images/stellar/prod/spellman2.jpg?c=original&q=w_860,c_fill)

“When the sirens sounded, she went to the basement of her building,” Spellman said.

When her niece returned to her apartment, “she had to push her way inside because the tornado had thrown all of her furniture to the far walls.”

They helped clean up after the storm passed and had to park over a mile away due to road closures, Spellman said. Dirt, glass and debris from trees and nearby homes coated everything inside the apartment and building. It took more than four hours to secure her niece’s apartment, clean it and remove her necessary belongings before dark.

![Image 5: A man helps remove the debris Saturday after a tornado struck in St. Louis.](https://media.cnn.com/api/v1/images/stellar/prod/2025-05-17t204500z-1054720436-rc2rjeaqcky6-rtrmadp-3-usa-weather.jpg?c=original&q=w_860,c_fill)

Another resident, Joan Miller Hitt, was in her home Friday when it was torn apart like a dollhouse.

When a large tree outside started swaying violently and all the doors shut like in the movie “Carrie,” Miller Hitt and her husband took shelter in a bathroom. Seconds later, “the whole back of the house was gone.”

Miller Hitt said she never saw it coming.

“I never had any fear of anything happening to that house with a storm because of where I live and the sound structure of the house,” she told CNN’s Fredricka Whitfield on Saturday afternoon. “I go between being overwhelmed, shocked, teary.”

Gov. Mike Kehoe said he has a﻿lready been in contact with federal officials about disaster relief. The American Red Cross opened three shelters in St. Louis for storm and tornado victims, the nonprofit [announced](https://www.stlouis-mo.gov/government/departments/public-safety/emergency-management/news/american-red-cross-shelters-open-following-tornado-damage-2025.cfm) Saturday.

First responders looking for victims or people in distress searched about 4,000 residences. More technical searches with boom microphones and cameras were being conducted Saturday.

One victim was identified as Patricia Pendleton, who had been serving lunches before the storm caused a roof to collapse at Centennial Christian Church, her family told [CNN affiliate KMOV](https://www.firstalert4.com/2025/05/16/4-fatalities-confirmed-due-storms-st-louis-area/).

![Image 6: Residents inspect their home after a tornado tore off the back wall of a two-story house in St. Louis.](https://media.cnn.com/api/v1/images/stellar/prod/2025-05-17t053951z-404741052-rc2ajea3jlfl-rtrmadp-3-usa-weather-st-louis.JPG?c=original&q=w_860,c_fill)

Sarah Russell, commissioner of the City Emergency Management Agency in St. Louis, said some of the tornado sirens did not go off Friday, which will be investigated.

“We’re looking into that,” she told reporters Saturday. The focus now is on life-saving measures in the community, she added.

The citywide system of tornado sirens was being replaced and had undergone testing on Thursday. Residents were encouraged to rely on multiple warning systems, including mobile apps and weather radio, she said.

The National Weather Service is surveying the damage and has no information on the intensity but estimated winds reached 100 mph.

Herzog’s message for residents: “I think the biggest thing would be staying away if you don’t need to be around.”

![Image 7: A house lies collapsed under a mountain of bricks, after a tornado struck in St. Louis, on Friday.](https://media.cnn.com/api/v1/images/stellar/prod/2025-05-17t043140z-1482064353-rc2cjeaf5vxi-rtrmadp-3-usa-weather-st-louis.jpg?c=original&q=w_860,c_fill)

As the system that hit Missouri and Kentucky weakens and pushes across the Southeast, another round of severe storms threatens the Great Plains and Texas.

The level 3 of 5 threat of severe storms will affect the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex Saturday evening, with large hail, damaging winds and the potential for tornadoes.

The possibility of more severe weather stretches through Tuesday in the Great Plains and the lower Mississippi River Valley.

The Plains will remain the main focus of severe weather on Sunday and Monday as well as the storms passing through Oklahoma and Kansas. The severe thunderstorm threat will then shift back into parts of the Mississippi Valley on Tuesday.

CNN’s Kelly Murray, Scott Withers, Phil Gast and Isaac Yee contributed to this report.

This page is about a tornado that struck the Kentucky communities of Somerset and London. For tornadoes in the namesake regions of England, see [Tornadoes in the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornadoes_in_the_United_Kingdom "Tornadoes in the United Kingdom").
2025 Somerset–London tornado

Clockwise from top: A photo of the tornado in Somerset, The Sunshine Hills Baptist Church in London swept away at low-end EF4 intensity, Violent tree debarking and stubbing in the Daniel Boone National Forest, Deeply pronounced "damage scar" through the Daniel Boone National Forest, imaged by Sentinel-2 on May 23, A home northwest of Mount Victory was leveled by the tornado

Meteorological history
FormedMay 16, 2025, 10:27 p.m. EDT (UTC–04:00)
DissipatedMay 16, 2025, 11:56 p.m. EDT (UTC-04:00)
Duration1 hour, 29 minutes[1]
EF4 tornado
on the Enhanced Fujita scale
Max width1,700 yards (0.97 mi; 1.6 km)
Path length60.08 miles (96.69 km)
Highest winds170 mph (270 km/h)
Overall effects
Fatalities19
Injuries108
Damage$350 million (2025 USD)
(Laurel County only)
Areas affectedRussell County, Pulaski County (specifically Somerset), Laurel County (specifically London)
Part of the tornado outbreak of May 15–16, 2025 and Tornadoes of 2025
In the late evening hours of May 16, 2025, a large and deadly [nocturnal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nocturnal_tornado "Nocturnal tornado") [EF4 tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced_Fujita_Scale "Enhanced Fujita Scale") moved through the [Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky "Kentucky") cities of [Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerset,_Kentucky "Somerset, Kentucky") and [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London,_Kentucky "London, Kentucky"). The tornado, which was on the ground for almost an hour and a half, killed 19 people and injured 108 others along a 60 mi (97 km) track. The tornado produced damage that was rated EF4 by the [National Weather Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Weather_Service "National Weather Service") in [Jackson, Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Kentucky "Jackson, Kentucky"). This violent tornado occurred as part of a [major tornado outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_May_15%E2%80%9316,_2025 "Tornado outbreak of May 15–16, 2025") that spanned from May 15 to 16. The [supercell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell "Supercell") that produced this tornado initiated over 400 miles (640 km) away in the south-central Missouri Ozarks region. The supercell produced few tornadoes along its track through Missouri, Illinois, and Kentucky, including a small but intense EF3 tornado that brought destructive impacts to the area south of the village of [Blodgett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blodgett,_Missouri "Blodgett, Missouri"), several homes suffered major damage, mobile homes were destroyed, trees were snapped. Two fatalities occurred and ten others were injured. Afterwards, the supercell crossed the [Ohio River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River "Ohio River") into [Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky "Kentucky"). The supercell produced a brief EF1 tornado near [Lamasco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamasco,_Kentucky "Lamasco, Kentucky") and an EF2 tornado near [Allegre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegre,_Kentucky "Allegre, Kentucky"), damaging or destroying several mobile homes and outbuildings. After the London tornado dissipated, the supercell eventually got absorbed into the [mesoscale convective system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoscale_convective_system "Mesoscale convective system").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Somerset%E2%80%93London_tornado#cite_note-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Somerset%E2%80%93London_tornado#cite_note-3) The tornado first touched down in central Russell County, initially causing minor damage to trees and infrastructure before quickly intensifying to EF3 strength, inflicting major damage to a home near Whittle. The tornado weakened and shrunk after crossing into Pulaski County. After crossing Lake Cumberland, the tornado struck the southern side of Somerset at low-end EF3 intensity, inflicting severe to major damage to several homes and businesses. After leaving the city, the tornado tore through parts of the [Daniel Boone National Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Boone_National_Forest "Daniel Boone National Forest") at mid-range EF3 to low-end EF4 intensity, shredding and snapping several trees and destroying a couple of homes as the tornado entered [Laurel County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_County,_Kentucky "Laurel County, Kentucky"). The tornado then impacted the southern side of London at low-end EF4 intensity, inflicting catastrophic destruction to several homes and neighborhoods, resulting in several fatalities. The tornado dissipated shortly after near the community of Lida. The tornado was on the ground for 90 minutes and tracked for 60 miles (97 km). Recovery efforts immediately following the tornado were intensive, with several aid organizations, including [The Salvation Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Salvation_Army "The Salvation Army") and the [Federal Emergency Management Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Emergency_Management_Agency "Federal Emergency Management Agency"), traveling to London with relief supplies. Following the tornado, media outlets claimed [National Weather Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Weather_Service_Jackson,_Kentucky "National Weather Service Jackson, Kentucky") office in [Jackson, Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Kentucky "Jackson, Kentucky") was [understaffed due to the staffing cuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NOAA_under_the_second_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "NOAA under the second presidency of Donald Trump") made by [Department of Government Efficiency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Government_Efficiency "Department of Government Efficiency"), although the office was fully staffed at the same time of the tornado. Meteorological synopsis ----------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2025_Somerset%E2%80%93London_tornado&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Meteorological synopsis")\] On May 12, the Storm Prediction Center outlined a Day 5 risk for middle [Mississippi River valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River_valley "Mississippi River valley"). A pacific front associated with May 15 convection was expected to stall across the middle Mississippi and lower [Ohio Valleys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Valley "Ohio Valley") before moving north as a potent warm front. Ensemble Guidance models at the time were hinting at dewpoints reaching between mid to upper 60s, possibly reaching into low 70s, with the likelihood of one or more linear segments to traverse across the mid-Mississippi, lower Ohio, to potentially into [Tennessee valleys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_Valley "Tennessee Valley").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Somerset%E2%80%93London_tornado#cite_note-4) On May 14 at 0730 UTC, The Storm Prediction Center outlined a slight (2/5) risk over much of the [Ozark Plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozark_Plateau "Ozark Plateau"), Mississippi and Ohio River Valleys, with possibility of seeing scattered discrete supercells, organized clusters, including the chance of a long-lived mesoscale convective system. Medium and long-range guidance model suggest the development of thunderstorms along the warm front, with a surface trough ahead of the mid-level wave will mature. The models depicted an environment where the mean level [convective available potential energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convective_available_potential_energy "Convective available potential energy") (MLCAPE) values were around 3000 J/kg and effective bulk shear of 40-50kn, developing a potent environment, with thermodynamic/kinematic conditions supporting development of long-lived severe weather. Despite this, there were still uncertainties around the event, with persistent disagreement among models still evident in regards to the northward extent of the warm sector, with some recent model runs showing the likelihood of persistent morning convection, and other model runs showing less morning convection.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Somerset%E2%80%93London_tornado#cite_note-5) [![Image 6: A map of CONUS, with different colors overlapping parts of states meaning different risk level. Red indicated MDT, orange ENH, yellow SLGT, dark green MRGL and light green TSTM.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/May_16%2C_2025_1300_UTC_Day_1_Convective_Outlook.gif/250px-May_16%2C_2025_1300_UTC_Day_1_Convective_Outlook.gif)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:May_16,_2025_1300_UTC_Day_1_Convective_Outlook.gif) [Storm Prediction Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_Prediction_Center "Storm Prediction Center") outlook issued at 1300 UTC on May 16, 2025, outlining a moderate risk for the [Ohio Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Valley "Ohio Valley") In the evening hours on the same day at 1730 UTC, an enhanced (3/5) risk was outlined for most of lower Ohio Valley, with one or more organized cluster and couple more discrete supercells. An upper-level trough over the southern [High Plains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Plains_/(United_States/) "High Plains (United States)") will traverse quickly across the Midwest, strong mid to upper southwesterly flow will overspread the region, the 500 mb jet stream was forecasted to be around 70-90kn. On May 16, 2025, a deadly 60 mile long tornado struck southeastern Kentucky. This was part of a broader tornado outbreak, but the effects of the Somerset-London tornado for the Daniel Boone National Forest were especially notable because of its EF3 to EF4 intensity.

Satellite imagery is an excellent tool for revealing the footprint of wind impacts, but assessment is needed to accurately map damage to deciduous and mixed deciduous-conifer forests. Some imagery is of sufficiently high resolution to resolve fallen trees directly, but without that, _change in foliage_ is our best indicator. However, leaves are absent for hardwoods prior to green-up, while conifers, like pine and hemlock, are good indicators of structural damage year-round. Moreover, during the growing season, moderate wind speeds often strip the foliage off hardwoods without causing meaningful structural damage. This means that regardless of the season, the initial pattern of observed change may reflect species composition as much as actual tree damage. In winter assessments, severe hardwood damage may be under-represented, and when conducted in the growing season damage may be over-represented. Fortunately, analysts have another powerful measure with streaming satellite technology, and that is the _persistence_ of the disturbance. Leaf stripping in spring is often manifest as a delay in green-up relative to adjacent undisturbed areas with full recovery by early to mid summer. Meanwhile, true crown damage in hardwoods should persist longer, often for the entire growing season or for multiple years.

Note the fine-resolution pattern of effects on slide 5. This recent logging unit largely showed an increase in NDVI over the last year despite being in the tornado track because it is in successional recovery. Scattered declines within the unit suggest there was some tornado damage, but the influence of multiple disturbances at short and longer time scales are revealed by this technology.

LONDON, Ky. (WKRC) — A powerful tornado tore through south-central Kentucky on Friday night, claiming the lives of at least 19 people, with 17 fatalities reported in Laurel County alone. The EF-3 tornado touched down in Somerset, Pulaski County, before wreaking havoc across the region, including London.

Jacob Jackson, who was at home with his grandmother near Old Whitley Road when the storm struck, said, "I couldn't be more grateful just to be standing here. Everything else, there's a lot of people around us that got hurt bad, so I just thank God, you know. He's really the only reason I'm standing here."

Nearby, Tina Carnes was on the phone with her family as the tornado hit.

> "We've lost everything. We don't have clothes, we don't have shoes, we don't have food, we don't I mean we don't there's nothing. I just I don't know what to do," she said.

Her sister's mobile home across the street was completely destroyed.

Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear toured the damage in Laurel County by car and helicopter on Saturday. He noted that this is the 13th major weather disaster to hit the state during his tenure, including other tornadoes in 2021 and major flooding earlier this year.

> "And we can't know why we keep getting hit over and over and over. Kentucky has gotten knocked down more times than just about anybody. We've gotten up every single time," Beshear said.

Governor Beshear also mentioned that he has been in contact with Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and praised the efforts of state and federal emergency management leaders. He vowed to ensure survivors receive as much state and federal funding as possible.

One of the victims was a major in the Laurel County Fire Department, who was responding to the storm at the time. Gov. Beshear warned that the death toll could rise as some victims remain in critical condition.
